LESSON: LISTENING AND SPEAKING 12.1.1 PUNCTUATION AND VOCABULARY

Grade: SNE  /  visual-impairment / Grade three
Subject: ENGLISH
Strand: Food and Diseases Suggested vocabulary Enough, harm, cough, warm, vegetables, fr
Topic 12.1: Listening and Speaking 12.1.1 Punctuation and Vocabulary
Suggested lessons in curriculum: 2

SECTION 1: INTRODUCTION

This lesson covers Listening and Speaking 12.1.1 Punctuation and Vocabulary, part of Food and Diseases Suggested vocabulary Enough, harm, cough, warm, vegetables, fr in SNE  /  visual-impairment / Grade three ENGLISH.

Key inquiry question: Why should we listen attentively?

You will study the official KICD learning outcomes, classroom activities, values, and competencies for this topic. Use Kenyan examples from your county, school, and community throughout.

SECTION 2: LEARNING OUTCOMES

By the end of this topic, you should be able to:

A. recognise the target letter- sound combinations (gr- pr- , -ew’) in given words,

   Learning focus: This outcome is part of Listening and Speaking 12.1.1 Punctuation and Vocabulary in the Kenya CBC curriculum.
   In class: Your teacher will guide you to discuss, practise, and demonstrate this skill using examples from Kenya.
   At home: Explain this point to a parent using an example from your school, home, or community.

B. pronounce words with the target letter-sound combinations,

   Learning focus: This outcome is part of Listening and Speaking 12.1.1 Punctuation and Vocabulary in the Kenya CBC curriculum.
   In class: Your teacher will guide you to discuss, practise, and demonstrate this skill using examples from Kenya.
   At home: Explain this point to a parent using an example from your school, home, or community.

C. use vocabulary related to the theme in the relevant context,

   Learning focus: This outcome is part of Listening and Speaking 12.1.1 Punctuation and Vocabulary in the Kenya CBC curriculum.
   In class: Your teacher will guide you to discuss, practise, and demonstrate this skill using examples from Kenya.
   At home: Explain this point to a parent using an example from your school, home, or community.

D. enjoy listening attentively and responding appropriately for effective communication. • Learners are guided to listen attentively for the target letter sounds combinations (gr- pr- , -ew’) in different words from an audio recording, • Learners are guided to say words with the target letter sound combination and record using a digital device with assistive technology, • Learners are guided to listen to the new words in short sentences/short paragraphs/teacher-read stories and write them down. • Learners are guided to collaboratively give the meaning of the words based on the context. • Learners with low vision are guided to practise new words in response to picture cues while learners with blindness are guided to practise new words in response to picture description cues. • Learners are guided to dramatise scenarios using the vocabulary words to talk about food and diseases. Why should we listen attentively? 89 • Learners with low vision are guided to practise the new words in a language game of matching vocabulary and pictures while learners with blindness fish out braille cards with the target vocabulary.

SECTION 4: LEARNING ACTIVITIES

A. At school

Follow your teacher’s guidance for group work, discussion, and practice on this topic.

B. At home with your parent or guardian

1. Read this lesson on Listening and Speaking 12.1.1 Punctuation and Vocabulary together.
2. Discuss the key inquiry question and give examples from your area.
3. Write five sentences summarising what you learned.
4. Prepare for the revision quiz at the end of this topic.

SECTION 5: CORE COMPETENCIES, VALUES, AND PCIs

Core Competencies to be developed:
• Communication and collaboration: The learner’s ability to listen keenly and actively is developed as they listen to oral texts, recognises words with

the target letter-sounds and pronounces them correctly.

• Digital literacy: The learner’s ability to interact with digital technology is improved as they say words with the target letter sound combination and

record using a digital device with assistive technology.

Values:
• Responsibility: Accountability is inculcated as the learner collaboratively gives the meaning of the words based on the context.

Pertinent and Contemporary Issues:
• Life skills (Self-esteem): The learner’s self-esteem is boosted as they use vocabulary learnt to talk about food and diseases.

Link to other Learning Areas:

The learner links the vocabulary learnt to learning of similar concepts in other learning areas.

Suggested Learning Resources

• Print textbooks in appropriate font size and colour contrast

• Braille books

• Digital devices with assistive technology,

• Charts, flash cards or braille cards,

• Pictures or picture description

Main points to remember:

1. recognise the target letter- sound combinations (gr- pr- , -ew’) in given words,
2. pronounce words with the target letter-sound combinations,
3. use vocabulary related to the theme in the relevant context,
4. enjoy listening attentively and responding appropriately for effective communication. • Learners are guided to listen attentively for the target letter sounds combinations (gr- pr- , -ew’) in different words from an audio recording, • Learners are guided to say words with the target letter sound combination and record using a digital device with assistive technology, • Learners are guided to listen to the new words in short sentences/short paragraphs/teacher-read stories and write them down. • Learners are guided to collaboratively give the meaning of the words based on the context. • Learners with low vision are guided to practise new words in response to picture cues while learners with blindness are guided to practise new words in response to picture description cues. • Learners are guided to dramatise scenarios using the vocabulary words to talk about food and diseases. Why should we listen attentively? 89 • Learners with low vision are guided to practise the new words in a language game of matching vocabulary and pictures while learners with blindness fish out braille cards with the target vocabulary.
